title: Hanuman's first words
hookLine: a hand or something harsh, one breath apart, and a stranger whose first words won Rama
carry: speech is tapas: true, kind and helpful
tomorrow: it's Nani's birthday. why doesn't she need to read the card?

cards: The same word can land two ways. Fine. Fine.
One is a shrug, the other a slammed door. Sanskrit builds that into its letters: kara can mean a hand; add a puff of breath after the k, kha, and khara means harsh. One breath apart.
The tradition cares a great deal about how words land, and one of its best-loved stories is about a first conversation that went exactly right.

teach.b: In the Ramayana, Rama and his brother Lakshmana are searching the forest for Sita when a stranger comes toward them, dressed as a wandering ascetic. It's Hanuman, sent by the monkey king Sugriva to find out who they are.
He speaks. And before Rama answers, he turns to his brother, amazed.
This one must know the Vedas, he says; in everything he said, not one word was wrong.
Not too long, not unclear, not rushed or halting, spoken from the chest and throat in an even voice; words that would win over even an enemy with a raised sword.
Out of that first exchange comes the friendship that carries Rama to Sita.

teach.h: THE GITA: THE TAPAS OF SPEECH.
teach.b: The Bhagavad Gita gives that kind of speech a name.

teach.h: TRUE, PLEASANT, BENEFICIAL, ALL AT ONCE.
teach.b: Krishna calls it the tapas, the discipline, of speech: words that cause no agitation, that are true, pleasant and beneficial, along with regular recitation of holy texts. All of it at once. True, but also kind.
Kind, but also useful. So for Hindus, how you speak isn't only manners; it's a practice, a tapas as real as a fast.
And when something goes out with too much breath behind it, a text, a comment, a reply in a group chat, the Gita doesn't scold. It gives a shape to try again.

how: Teachers of Sanskrit and Hindi often have students hold a hand or a slip of paper before the mouth to feel the difference between unaspirated and aspirated consonants such as ka and kha.

games.q: a group chat is getting heated, and you've typed a reply that's true but sharp. what fits the Gita's discipline of speech?
o: keep it true, but rewrite it so it's kind and actually helps.
send it: if it's true, how it lands isn't your problem.
say nothing true at all; just agree, to keep the peace.
games.why: the Gita asks for all of it at once: true, pleasant and beneficial. not truth alone, and not pleasantness alone.

practice: Hold your palm a few inches from your lips and say ka, then kha, and feel the second one land on your skin. Then rest the hand in your lap and think of one thing you need to say to someone this week.
Hold it up to the Gita's three: is it true, is it kind, will it help? Breathe out softly, with no puff at all, until you know how to say it.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: some made with a little breath, some with a great one, and words that change with the puff.

orig.note: Sanskrit: heat, discipline; the Gita names a tapas of the body, of speech and of the mind.

carryVoice: Carry this: speech is tapas, true and kind and helpful, all at once. Go gently.
